# x0k-timeline

Every process on your machine logs somewhere different. When something goes
wrong across three of them, you open three files and line up timestamps by
hand.

`x0k-timeline` is one small service that takes the spans, logs and events of
every process on a machine and keeps them in one store, so you can ask one
question of all of them. Anything that can send OpenTelemetry over HTTP can
write to it, in any language, with no library of ours. You read it with SQL
from the command line, or through tools an AI agent can call over MCP.

Your records stay on your machine. The service binds to loopback and sends
nothing anywhere.

## Run it

```sh
cargo install --locked x0k-timeline
x0k-timeline
```

That is all a build needs: Rust. From a clone, `cargo run --release --bin
x0k-timeline` does the same on the release `rust-toolchain.toml` names, the one
CI uses. With no arguments the program is the service. One instance runs per
state directory, and a second refuses to start.

To keep it running after a crash or a reboot, hand it to your machine's service
manager:

```sh
x0k-timeline service install
```

`uninstall`, `start`, `stop` and `status` do what they say. It installs a user
service where the manager has them, and takes the `X0K_` settings of the shell you
ran it in. systemd restarts it after a crash, and leaves it stopped if you stopped
it. launchd keeps it running whatever the reason it ended. Windows has no user
services here, so `install` needs an administrator, and restarts are limited.
Only the systemd path has been exercised so far.

It listens on two loopback ports:

| Port | What it serves |
|---|---|
| 4318 | OTLP over HTTP, the port exporters default to |
| 3456 | The query tools over MCP (streamable HTTP) |

## Write to it

Point any OpenTelemetry exporter at it, using the JSON encoding:

```sh
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:4318
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/json
```

Traces, logs and metrics are taken at `/v1/traces`, `/v1/logs` and
`/v1/metrics`. Protobuf is refused with a 415, and nothing is written.

A Rust process can link `x0k-timeline-emit` instead, with its `auto-persist`
feature, and gets something OTLP cannot give it: if the service is down, its spans
go to a segment on disk and are sent when the service comes back, so a crash at boot
still leaves a record of the boot.

```toml
[dependencies]
x0k-timeline-emit = { version = "=0.2.0", features = ["auto-persist"] }
```

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use tracing_subscriber::layer::SubscriberExt;
use x0k_timeline_emit::observability::ObservabilityLayer;
use x0k_timeline_emit::span_tracing::{
    run_timeline_forwarder_task, ChannelSpanSink, TimelineEndpoint,
};
use x0k_timeline_emit::timeline_channel::take_timeline_receiver;

let endpoint = TimelineEndpoint::for_profile(socket_path, &profile_dir);
let receiver = take_timeline_receiver().expect("taken once");
tokio::spawn(run_timeline_forwarder_task(receiver, endpoint));

let layer = ObservabilityLayer::builder()
    .with_span_sink(Arc::new(ChannelSpanSink::new()))
    .build();
tracing::subscriber::set_global_default(tracing_subscriber::registry().with(layer))?;
```

`socket_path` is the service's socket and `profile_dir` is its directory under
`$X0K_HOME/profiles/`. This crate has no stable API yet, so pin it.

A program you cannot change can still write here:

```sh
x0k-timeline run -- ./worker --port 8080
```

Its output still reaches your terminal, each line is a record, and how it ended
is a record, even if the service was down at the time: those wait in a segment
and arrive when it comes back. `run` leaves with the program's exit code and does
no restarts. The one cost is that the program writes to a pipe rather than a
terminal, so some programs buffer their output or drop their colours.

A process cannot report its own death, so anything watching it can do that
instead, which is what `run` does. Send an OTLP log record named `process.exit`, with `process.pid`,
`timeline.process.cause` and `timeline.process.oom`, and the attributes you know.
The record's own process is the observer. It is kept for as long as an event
rather than a log, because it is the evidence left when the logs are gone.
Section 8 of the public-surface decision has the full shape.

## Read it

From a shell:

```sh
x0k-timeline query \
  "SELECT timestamp_us, entry_kind, level, span_name, description FROM timeline ORDER BY timestamp_us DESC LIMIT 20" --table
```

This runs without the service and needs no lock. It reads rows that have not
reached a Parquet file yet, so what just happened is there.

An agent, or anything else that speaks MCP, connects to port 3456 and has
these tools:

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `query_timeline_sql` | Runs one read-only `SELECT` over the store |
| `describe_timeline` | Says what the columns are, which event families the store holds, and whether the service is paused |
| `query_call_stack` | Rebuilds the call tree of one trace |
| `pause_timeline` | Stops keeping spans, logs and events, and says why |
| `resume_timeline` | Starts keeping them again |

Nobody writes a schema for what you send. Every file the service writes
records, for each event family it holds, the fields that family carried, their
types, where they were emitted from and when the family was first and last seen.
Name a family in `describe_timeline` and it answers from those records and from
rows not yet in a file. A field sent as a number in one place and as text in
another is reported as a conflict rather than coerced, so you find the mismatch
before a query does.

A pause is itself written down. The rows `timeline.paused` and
`timeline.resumed` are kept, with a count of what was discarded, so a gap in
the timeline reads as a gap and not as a stretch where nothing happened.
Programs sending records see no failure while the service is paused.

## Configure it

Everything comes from the environment.

| Variable | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `X0K_HOME` | The state root | `~/.0k` |
| `X0K_PROFILE` | The directory under `profiles/`; two profiles are two services | `main` |
| `X0K_TIMELINE_OTLP_PORT` | The OTLP port | `4318` |
| `X0K_TIMELINE_QUERY_MCP_LISTEN` | The MCP address | `127.0.0.1:3456` |
| `X0K_TIMELINE_SOCKET` | The local writer socket | `x0k-timeline.sock` in the profile directory |
| `X0K_TIMELINE_PAUSED` | `1` or `true` starts the service paused | not paused |

## What it promises

This is release 0.3. It promises the OTLP ingest, the SQL surface, the tool
names, the record format they return, and what a process observation must carry. The promises are
written down in
[the public-surface decision](decisions/architecture/substrate/timeline-public-surface.md).

It does not promise a Rust API. The crates here are how the service is built,
and they can change in any release. They are on crates.io because the service
installs from there and a Rust process links one of them.

That decision describes where this is going, and more of it than this release
builds. These are not here yet, whatever it says:

- A view per event family. `describe_timeline` tells you a family's fields, and you
  query them with `json_extract(fields_json, '$.name')`.
- `export_chrome_trace`, the export to Perfetto.
- Ingest as canonical CBOR frames. A process writes through OTLP/HTTP or the emit
  crate, and the socket between the emit crate and the service carries no promise.
- Segments in canonical CBOR. They are postcard today. A segment's first frame names
  its format, so a later release reads an old one or leaves it on disk and says why.
- The base reader, which reads segments with a CBOR codec alone.
- An application's state history as a row.

`crates/x0k-timeline/vectors/` holds the conformance vectors: files any
implementation of these promises can run. The vectors say what a writer
accepts and refuses, how an OTLP request maps to records, how a torn segment
reads back, how a pause behaves, and which process observations are kept and
which are refused. `cargo test -p x0k-timeline --test
conformance` runs them here, and says `NOT RUN` by name for any check this
release does not hold.

## Reading the implementation

Most of the Rust here is ordinary source. The parts listed below are written
as chapters under `implementation/`, which explain the code and generate it.
Change the chapter, not the generated file.

**What it ships.** Every chapter, grouped by what it is about rather than which crate its code lands in.

### The record

The record every process writes: its fields, how it is stored and how it reads back.

- [x0k-timeline-record: the types the timeline owns](implementation/substrate/timeline-record.md) — x0k-timeline-record: the record, span, ingest and trace-override types the timeline's emitter, writer and reader share, in a crate that depends on no x0k type, so the timeline can stand without x0k-types.

### The local socket

How a client reaches a service on the same machine.

- [Local IPC belongs to its service](implementation/local-ipc/local-ipc.md) — How a client on one machine reaches a service: the endpoint belongs to the service, and the transport is a Unix socket or a Windows named pipe.

## Where it comes from

This repository is projected from [x0k](https://0k.computer), a local-first
system that runs the same service. A change proposed here comes back as a
proposal against x0k's sources and appears in this repository on the next
projection.
